blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 17 (Human Reproductive System), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, compare, label and describe a structure, give examples), as one 4-mark part or in 1+3 / 2+2 sub-parts. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 Reproduction produces offspring of the same type. (i) Give the functions of the male and female reproductive systems. (ii) How is the reproductive system different from other organ systems? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Reproduction is the ability of an organism to produce new offspring of its own type.

(i) Functions:
1. Both systems produce reproductive cells (gametes) and prepare them for fertilization.
2. The male system delivers the gametes to the female reproductive system.
3. The female system nourishes the fertilized egg cell and provides an environment for its development into a baby.

(ii) Differences from other organ systems:
1. The reproductive system is quite different in male and female, while the other organ systems are almost the same in both.
2. It does not become functional until puberty, whereas all other systems are functional since or shortly after birth.

book_ref.quote: The functions of reproductive systems include the production of reproductive cells (gametes)

blocks.prompt: 2 Describe the position and internal structure of the testes, including the cells found in and between the seminiferous tubules and the importance of the scrotum. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Position: two testes lie outside the abdomen in a skin pouch, the scrotum. They form in the abdominal cavity during development and descend into the scrotum shortly before birth. The scrotum keeps them at about 34°C, slightly below core body temperature (37°C); this lower temperature is required for sperm development.

Structure: each testis is oval, about 3–5 cm long and 2–3 cm wide, and is composed of highly convoluted seminiferous tubules.
1. Germinal epithelium (wall of the tubules) has two types of cells:
a. Germline cells: make sperms by meiosis.
b. Sertoli cells: nourish developing sperms; their fluid carries non-motile sperms into the epididymis; under FSH they release inhibin.
2. Leydig cells: in the interstitial tissue between the tubules; under LH they secrete testosterone.
3. From the tubules, sperms pass into the rete testis and then the epididymis.

book_ref.quote: A testis is composed of highly convoluted seminiferous tubules

blocks.prompt: 3 Describe the process of spermatogenesis, showing the chromosome number at each stage. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Spermatogenesis is the process by which sperms are formed inside the seminiferous tubules of the testes.
1. Germline cells (2n) in the walls of the tubules divide by mitosis. Some new cells become spermatogonia (2n); others remain germline cells for future use.
2. Spermatogonia (2n) continue to divide and form primary spermatocytes (2n), which move toward the lumen of the tubules.
3. Each primary spermatocyte divides by meiosis-I to form two secondary spermatocytes (1n).
4. These quickly undergo meiosis-II to produce spermatids (1n).
So one spermatogonium (2n) produces four spermatids (1n).
5. Each spermatid matures into an elongated sperm.
Control: FSH (from the anterior pituitary under GnRH) stimulates the seminiferous tubules for spermatogenesis.

book_ref.quote: In the walls of seminiferous tubules, special cells called germline cells (2n) divide by mitosis

blocks.prompt: 4 Describe the structure of a mature sperm. How does it reach the epididymis and become motile? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Structure: a sperm has three parts.
1. Head: contains the genetic material. About two-thirds of it is covered by a thick cap, the acrosome, formed mainly of Golgi body; it contains enzymes that later help the sperm to fertilize the ovum.
2. Midpiece: contains mitochondria and a centriole.
3. Tail: formed of microtubules (axial filament) arising from the centriole of the midpiece.

Maturation: mature spermatozoa in the lumen of the seminiferous tubules are non-motile. They pass (through the rete testis) into the epididymis with the help of fluid secreted by Sertoli cells. In the epididymis they remain at least 18 hours and gain motility; they then enter the vas deferens.

book_ref.quote: The genetic material is present within its head

blocks.prompt: 5 Explain how negative feedback keeps the levels of FSH and LH under control in the male. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Spermatogenesis is controlled by hormones of the hypothalamus and pituitary gland.
1. The hypothalamus releases GnRH, which stimulates the anterior pituitary to release FSH and LH.
2. FSH stimulates the seminiferous tubules for spermatogenesis. FSH also causes the Sertoli cells to release a peptide hormone, inhibin, which inhibits further FSH secretion.
3. LH stimulates Leydig cells (in the interstitial tissue) to secrete testosterone. Testosterone stimulates development of the germinal epithelium and maintains male secondary sexual characteristics.
4. The rising testosterone inhibits the release of LH and GnRH.
Thus each pituitary hormone causes a product (inhibin or testosterone) that switches off its own further release: negative feedback.

book_ref.quote: Similarly, when LH stimulates Leydig cells to secrete testosterone

blocks.prompt: 6 Compare the male and female gonads with respect to position, size, structure and products. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: The gonads are the testes (male) and ovaries (female). They are compared in the table.

book_ref.quote: There are two ovaries – each present on the side of the uterus

blocks.prompt: 7 The ovary releases an egg each month. (i) Describe the ovary and its follicles. (ii) Describe the oviducts and the events that take place in them. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Ovaries produce egg cells (ova or oocytes) and release hormones. There are two, one on each side of the uterus; each is oval, 3-5 cm long and 2-3 cm wide. It contains many tiny sac-like ovarian follicles, the functional units of the ovary, which nurture immature eggs. In an adult female, one ripening follicle ejects its egg each month (ovulation). The ruptured follicle becomes a glandular structure, the corpus luteum.

(ii) The oviducts (fallopian or uterine tubes) are two tubes leading from the ovaries into the uterus.
1. When an ovum matures, the follicle and ovary wall rupture to release it, and it enters an oviduct.
2. It travels toward the uterus, helped by the movements of cilia on the inner lining of the oviduct.
3. Fertilization of the ovum occurs in the oviduct; there the secondary oocyte completes meiosis-II.
4. The zygote undergoes several mitotic divisions while still in the oviduct.

blocks.prompt: 8 Describe the parts of the uterus and the layers of its wall. How is the placenta formed? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
The uterus is a hollow, muscular organ into which the two oviducts open.

Parts:
1. Fundus: uppermost rounded portion above the openings of the oviducts.
2. Body: the major portion.
3. Cervix: lower narrow part; its opening leads to the vagina (an 8-10 cm thin-walled tube to the outside).

Layers of the wall:
1. Perimetrium: outermost thin layer.
2. Myometrium: middle thick layer of smooth muscles.
3. Endometrium: inner spongy lining with a basal layer (stem cells that regenerate the functional layer) and a functional layer (thickens and is shed in each menstrual cycle).

Placenta: during pregnancy the functional layer thickens further to implant the embryo. Its vascular spaces fuse and become interconnected, forming the placenta, which supplies oxygen and nutrition to the embryo and foetus.

book_ref.quote: The two oviducts enter into a hollow and muscular organ called uterus

blocks.prompt: 9 Describe oogenesis from the embryonic stage to the formation of the ovum. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Oogenesis (production of the ovum) starts during the embryonic development of the female.
1. Embryonic stage: oogonia (2n) in the follicles divide by mitosis to produce primary oocytes (2n). These begin meiosis-I but stop in prophase-I, and remain so all through childhood (at least 10 to 14 years). At birth the ovaries contain some 2 million follicles, each with a primary oocyte.
2. Puberty: only one of the many primary oocytes resumes meiosis-I and produces two dissimilar haploid cells: the larger secondary oocyte (1n) and the smaller first polar body (1n).
3. The secondary oocyte stops division in metaphase-II and is released from the ovary into the oviduct at ovulation.
4. If it is not fertilized, it dies. If a sperm fuses with it, it quickly completes meiosis-II in the oviduct, producing one large ovum (1n) and a small second polar body (1n).

book_ref.quote: In that period, the oogonia (2n) present in follicle divide by mitosis to produce primary oocytes (2n)

blocks.prompt: 10 Describe the changes that take place in the ovary during one menstrual cycle. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Menstrual phase (days 1-5): the gonadotropins and FSH begin to rise.
2. Follicle growth: due to the rise in FSH, a few ovarian follicles begin growing, but only one grows fully and the others degenerate. This mature follicle, the Graafian follicle, rises to the surface of the ovary. FSH stimulates it to secrete estrogen.
3. Ovulation (day 14): at the end of the proliferative phase the sudden release of LH from the anterior pituitary stimulates the Graafian follicle to release the ovum into the oviduct.
4. Corpus luteum (days 15-28): after ovulation, LH stimulates the ruptured Graafian follicle to develop into a yellow structure, the corpus luteum, which secretes estrogen and progesterone.
5. If fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum degenerates; if it occurs, hCG from the embryo maintains it.

book_ref.quote: Due to the rise in FSH, few ovarian follicles begin growing

blocks.prompt: 11 Describe the changes in the endometrium of the uterus during the three phases of the menstrual cycle, naming the hormones responsible. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
The menstrual cycle lasts about 28 days.
1. Menstrual phase (days 1-5): the functional layer of the endometrium is shed; the detached tissue and blood move out of the body (menstruation), for 3-5 days. Cause: low levels of estrogen and progesterone.
2. Proliferative phase (days 6-14): estrogen secreted by the Graafian follicle causes initial vascularization of the endometrium and makes it velvety and thick again. The phase ends with ovulation on day 14.
3. Secretory/post-ovulatory phase (days 15-28): estrogen and progesterone from the corpus luteum make the endometrium more vascular and glandular.
End of cycle: if fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum degenerates; estrogen and progesterone fall abruptly and the thickened endometrium is shed with bleeding (menstruation on day 28). The basal layer's stem cells later regenerate the functional layer.

book_ref.quote: In this phase, the functional layer of endometrium is shed

blocks.prompt: 12 The fate of the corpus luteum decides whether menstruation occurs. (i) What happens when the ovulated oocyte is not fertilized? (ii) What happens when it is fertilized, and why is hCG used in pregnancy tests? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
After ovulation, LH makes the ruptured Graafian follicle develop into the yellow corpus luteum, which secretes estrogen and progesterone and makes the endometrium more vascular and glandular.

(i) Not fertilized: the secondary oocyte dies. The corpus luteum starts to degenerate and the anterior pituitary no longer secretes LH. The destruction of the corpus luteum causes an abrupt fall in estrogen and progesterone, so the thickened endometrium is shed with bleeding: menstruation on day 28, and a new cycle begins.

(ii) Fertilized: the tiny embryo secretes human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), which maintains the corpus luteum. Estrogen and progesterone stay high and menstruation is prevented; the endometrium thickens further for implantation and forms the placenta. Because hCG comes from the embryonic chorion and not the mother, it is the hormone tested for in all pregnancy tests.

book_ref.quote: When the ovulated oocyte is fertilized, the tiny embryo secretes human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)
